newsitem.title: USA: New York joins battle against tobacco industry.
newsitem.headline: New York joins battle against tobacco industry.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, Law Correspondent
New York, the nation's most populous city, joined the nationwide battle against the tobacco industry Thursday by suing to recoup health care costs of smokers.

The suit, filed in New York State Supreme Court in Manhattan, seeks restitution and punitive damages to be determined at trial. Among allegations is that the industry committed fraud and violated the state's antitrust, deceptive trade practices and false advertising laws.
The strongly worded suit alleges that cigarette makers and their trade associations "pursued a conspiracy of deceit and misrepresentation" to hide the health risks of smoking.

"Defendants have also concealed from the public the fact that they manipulate and control the nicotine content and delivery of their products to create and sustain users' addiction to tobacco," the suit alleges.
The tobacco industry maintains that nicotine is not addictive and that it does not "spike" cigarettes.

New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani, who has long supported smoking control efforts, told a news conference that he expected Philip Morris Cos. Inc. to threaten to move its headquarters out of Manhattan because of the suit.
In 1994 the world's biggest tobacco company threatened to leave because of a proposed expansion of New York City's smoking restrictions. Guiliani said he was prepared for a similar reaction now.
"I'm never affected by people who threaten," he said. "If they want to leave the City of New York, we'll replace those jobs. I'm sure they will threaten us."
Philip Morris did not have an immediate comment.
However, R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. responded: "It would appear that Mayor Giuliani has conferred only with rabid antismokers and product liability lawyers before filing today's suit.

"We regret that he didn't ask the tobacco industry at the very least to sit down and discuss the litigation before suing us," Reynolds said, adding that it believed there was a serious question about whether Giuliani has jurisdiction to bring such a case.
"The mayor may garner some political mileage out of this filing, but that will be all," Reynolds said.

The suit is seeking recovery of the cost of treating lung cancer and other tobacco-related diseseas in Medicaid patients and uninsured patients treated without charge in public hospitals. It also seeks reimbursement for tobacco-related costs of health benefits provided to city employees.

The suit cited a 1994 study that found the city spent about $300 million on health care costs related to tobacco use. It said this figure excludes indirect costs of tobacco use, such as loss of income from smokers who cannot work.
The suit is similar to those brought by 16 states in an attempt to force cigarette companies to reimburse them for health care costs of smokers.
San Francisco, Los Angeles, San Jose and 10 other counties in California have also sued the industry.

New York City, which has a population of about 7.8 million, will be the first city on the East coast to sue the tobacco industry. Erie County, which includes the city of Buffalo, previously said it expects to file a Medicaid suit shortly and has been attempting to get other New York counties to join with it.

The Coalition for a Smoke-Free City, which includes the American Cancer Society and the American Heart and the American Lung Associations, has been urging the mayor to file suit due to inaction by New York state Attorney General Dennis Vacco. A spokesman for Vacco had no immediate comment.

"The tobacco cartel has lied and misled the public about the dangers of tobacco addiction for decades. New York City's health care bill attributed to tobacco addiction exceeds $2 billion annually," the coalition said in a letter to Giuliani.

Richard Daynard, chairman of the Tobacco Products Liablity Project at Northeastern University in Boston, said the filing by New York City is significant because it shows that leaders of the biggest states and cities can no longer ignore efforts to seek reimbursement of health care costs of smokers.
"A public official today cannot refrain from collecting available funds for defraying this expense," Daynard said.
